2272441,ca.proc.d.1964-04-10.5.2.1.2,1964-04-10,84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089,ca.m.3212,Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):,Leader of the Official Opposition,BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,REQUEST FOR INCREASED NUMBER OF CANADIAN TROOPS,Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs arising out of certain questions asked yesterday and the suggestion on his part that Canada was giving consideration to providing additional forces to the United Nations force in Cyprus. Would he let the house know what the situation is in this connection? Also, does he agree with mounting public opinion to the effect that the willing shoulders of Canada are already bearing our share of the United Nations force, a larger share than that of any other nation, with the exception of the United Kingdom; that it has accepted its full and complete share, and that any additional troops should be provided by other members of the United Nations?

,Progressive Conservative,,John George Diefenbaker,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089&Language=E&Section=ALL
2272442,ca.proc.d.1964-04-10.5.2.1.3,1964-04-10,intervention,,,,BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,REQUEST FOR INCREASED NUMBER OF CANADIAN TROOPS,Hear, hear.

,,,Some hon. Members:,
2272443,ca.proc.d.1964-04-10.5.2.1.4,1964-04-10,dbc81dd3-47f7-4448-a205-ccbf43047e83,ca.m.8658,Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):,Secretary of State for External Affairs,BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,REQUEST FOR INCREASED NUMBER OF CANADIAN TROOPS,Mr. Speaker, in reply to the right hon. gentleman's question I can assure him, as I have already indicated elsewhere, that Canada does feel that other members of the United Nations ought to share in the obligations which are imposed on them under the charter of the United Nations.

I can confirm that we have received a request from the secretary general for additional personnel. We hope to be able to deal with this matter very shortly. The request we have received is not in the same category as that which has been addressed by the secretary general to the governments of Sweden, Finland and Ireland. The request to those governments is for additional ground troops and is part of the secretary general's attempts to bring the non-British component of the United Nations force up to the 3,500 level originally envisaged.
The request to Canada is for brigade headquarters staff, a ""function which up to now

has been discharged by United Kingdom forces. Both requests form part of the field reorganization which General Gyani is putting into effect as the international force is gradually phased in to take over some staff and peace keeping functions previously undertaken by British forces.

,Liberal,,Paul Joseph James Martin,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=dbc81dd3-47f7-4448-a205-ccbf43047e83&Language=E&Section=ALL
2272444,ca.proc.d.1964-04-10.5.2.1.5,1964-04-10,84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089,ca.m.3212,Mr. Diefenbaker:,Leader of the Official Opposition,BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,REQUEST FOR INCREASED NUMBER OF CANADIAN TROOPS,What would be the number of brigade staff that is being asked for; would it be less than 100?

,Progressive Conservative,,John George Diefenbaker,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089&Language=E&Section=ALL
2272445,ca.proc.d.1964-04-10.5.2.1.6,1964-04-10,dbc81dd3-47f7-4448-a205-ccbf43047e83,ca.m.8658,Mr. Martin (Essex East):,Secretary of State for External Affairs,BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,REQUEST FOR INCREASED NUMBER OF CANADIAN TROOPS,It would be slightly over 100 but less than 150.

,Liberal,,Paul Joseph James Martin,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=dbc81dd3-47f7-4448-a205-ccbf43047e83&Language=E&Section=ALL
2272446,ca.proc.d.1964-04-10.5.2.1.7,1964-04-10,84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089,ca.m.3212,Mr. Diefenbaker:,Leader of the Official Opposition,BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,REQUEST FOR INCREASED NUMBER OF CANADIAN TROOPS,Would the minister say what representations have been made to the secretary general requesting that he endeavour to secure forces from other members of the United Nations? Because it seems, in view of the course being followed now, that it is only the willing that provide and the unwilling stand by.

,Progressive Conservative,,John George Diefenbaker,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089&Language=E&Section=ALL
2272447,ca.proc.d.1964-04-10.5.2.1.8,1964-04-10,dbc81dd3-47f7-4448-a205-ccbf43047e83,ca.m.8658,Mr. Martin (Essex East):,Secretary of State for External Affairs,BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,REQUEST FOR INCREASED NUMBER OF CANADIAN TROOPS,Mr. Speaker, I am sure my hon. friend will recognize in that generalization he has simply expressed an impulse of human nature.

,Liberal,,Paul Joseph James Martin,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=dbc81dd3-47f7-4448-a205-ccbf43047e83&Language=E&Section=ALL

,,,Some hon. Members:,
2272449,ca.proc.d.1964-04-10.5.2.1.10,1964-04-10,370da791-e7ce-4318-b030-1863dd5185ee,ca.m.6774,Mr. Mandziuk:,,BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,REQUEST FOR INCREASED NUMBER OF CANADIAN TROOPS,Don't you share it?

,Progressive Conservative,,J. Nicholas (Nick) Mandziuk,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=370da791-e7ce-4318-b030-1863dd5185ee&Language=E&Section=ALL
2272450,ca.proc.d.1964-04-10.5.2.1.11,1964-04-10,dbc81dd3-47f7-4448-a205-ccbf43047e83,ca.m.8658,Mr. Martin (Essex East):,Secretary of State for External Affairs,BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,REQUEST FOR INCREASED NUMBER OF CANADIAN TROOPS,Canada, however, as he has properly noted, has not shirked its responsibilities. We have made strong representations to the secretary general of the United Nations that he should solicit, as indeed he is doing, the contributions of other countries. We ourselves only this morning have been engaged in that process with two other countries.

,Liberal,,Paul Joseph James Martin,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=dbc81dd3-47f7-4448-a205-ccbf43047e83&Language=E&Section=ALL
2272451,ca.proc.d.1964-04-10.5.2.1.12,1964-04-10,84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089,ca.m.3212,Mr. Diefenbaker:,Leader of the Official Opposition,BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,REQUEST FOR INCREASED NUMBER OF CANADIAN TROOPS,Mr. Speaker, may I thank the minister for the impulsive nature that he exercised in doing that.

,Progressive Conservative,,John George Diefenbaker,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089&Language=E&Section=ALL
2272452,ca.proc.d.1964-04-10.5.2.1.13,1964-04-10,2094cd47-759f-4f54-8d75-9da36dd888a2,ca.m.4073,Hon. Marcel Lamberi (Edmonton West):,,BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,REQUEST FOR INCREASED NUMBER OF CANADIAN TROOPS,Mr. Speaker, the minister mentioned a force of 3,500. I rather assume that he meant 7,500.

,Progressive Conservative,,Marcel Joseph Aimé Lambert,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=2094cd47-759f-4f54-8d75-9da36dd888a2&Language=E&Section=ALL
2272453,ca.proc.d.1964-04-10.5.2.1.14,1964-04-10,dbc81dd3-47f7-4448-a205-ccbf43047e83,ca.m.8658,Mr. Martin (Essex East):,Secretary of State for External Affairs,BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,REQUEST FOR INCREASED NUMBER OF CANADIAN TROOPS,I was referring to the desire, pursuant to the resolution of the security council, to reduce the British force from 7,000 to 3,500 and bring the United Nations force up to 3,500 to reach the total of 7,000, the maximum provided for in the security council resolution.

,Liberal,,Paul Joseph James Martin,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=dbc81dd3-47f7-4448-a205-ccbf43047e83&Language=E&Section=ALL

According to an article in Le Devoir this morning, the secretary general of the United
Nations is said to have asked Canada to send another Canadian unit to Cyprus in the near future.
Can the minister tell us what his intentions are in this respect?

,Ralliement Créditiste,,Raymond Langlois,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=184bb42b-3d9a-445d-a741-c2acec461ffd&Language=E&Section=ALL

Pickersgill (Minister of Transport):,Minister of Transport,TRANSPORT,FREIGHT RATES AND RAIL LINE ABANDONMENT,STATEMENT BY MINISTER,The hon. member's question is perhaps not terribly urgent since it relates to something which happened on April 3, but I should like to answer it, if I may, by saying that I am very grateful to the Canadian railway association for agreeing to continue for another three months the suspension, which has already been in operation for a long time, of a rate increase granted by the board of transport commissioners in the hope that in this three months interval parliament will be permitted to consider the legislation on railways which the government would like to introduce.

With respect to the second matter, may I say it is not, of course, the government which abandons railway lines. It is the railway companies which abandon them after they have been allowed to do so under the law. All I was doing was expressing my own opinion that because of the benevolent policies initiated by the government of hon. gentlemen opposite and continued by this government, the railways had indicated what lines they wished to abandon, but did not proceed with those applications until the new legislation could be dealt with by parliament. It would therefore appear that there would be no abandonments in a hurry. It is also my opinion that even after that time there would be no abandonments in a hurry, particularly when one thinks of the traffic which the railways are carrying in western Canada at the present time.

Pearson (Prime Minister):,Prime Minister,HEALTH AND WELFARE,TORONTO,HOSPITAL GRANT,I have the information, and I regret it has taken so long to answer the hon. member's question. This is a lengthy answer but it deals with a most important matter, so with the indulgence of the house I propose to read the reply.

The hon. member asked me to comment on the hospital shortage in Toronto and particularly the federal government's intent respecting federal construction grants to metropolitan Toronto hospitals. Hon. members are aware that the council of metropolitan Toronto and subsequently the council of Scarborough township spoke to ministers of the government-I believe they spoke to the Minister of National Health and Welfare- regarding an increase in bed grants within the last year. At the urging of members on this side of the house from the Toronto area, as well as some hon. members opposite, the government has studied the Agnew report indicating that hospital beds in the metropolitan area presently fall more than 2,000 short of requirements. This has been primarily caused by the population explosion in the Toronto suburbs and accentuated by the fact that the metropolitan government found it impossible to render assistance in this field from 1958 until earlier this year.

The federal government has for some months sought a fair way of assisting in a unique situation. Of course any solution would have to be on an across the country basis and not confined to one locality. The matter has been discussed with the responsible health ministers and in most cases with provincial premiers at the past two dominion-provincial meetings, without arriving at any solution. Indeed, more than one province has indicated strong disapproval of the suggestion of any proposed increase in grants, as providing increased pressure upon provincial treasuries to meet increased federal grants in a field which is considered primarily one of provincial responsibility.

Within the past few months the federal government, through the municipal loan fund, has assisted the municipal government to the extent of $29 million which has been used for projects other than hospital construction. In the opinion of the government, further federal assistance would not be warranted at this time.

Since 1948 more than $19,500,000 has been expended by the federal government for this purpose in metropolitan Toronto. The current commitment, extending for a five year period through to 1968, is augmented by a national health grant to help finance a home care program in metropolitan Toronto, announced on March 26 last, to take pressure off hospital beds for convalescents.
Inquiries of the Ministry

We understand, too, that the government of Ontario, in acknowledgement of its own special responsibility in the field, has developed a new program for low interest loans for construction in Ontario, intended to be of special assistance in the Toronto area.

2272652,ca.proc.d.1964-04-10.24.2,1964-04-10,84ed4838-0481-4feb-903d-e74c47997afa,ca.m.9475,Mr. Martineau:,,DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES,,,"Mr. Chairman, I am sorry that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) is not in the house this morning, because I wanted, first of all, to congratulate him. I wanted to commend him because yesterday, he achieved a really remarkable feat. Indeed, Mr. Chairman, he succeeded in displeasing everybody, while satisfying nobody. I hope to show how he did this.

For instance, let us take those who believe that jurisdiction over the Eskimos should be transferred from the federal to the provincial government; those people are certainly very dissatisfied with the philosophy expounded yesterday before the committee, by the Minister of Justice. Ottawa has a jurisdiction in this matter but, according to him, that jurisdiction is elusive, inefficient and often illusory-illusory because the federal government does not propose to exercise it.

How could this government sitting opposite give a clearer and more complete indication of its impotency, its weakness and confusion, than by insisting-with the support of a ruling made by the supreme court and of the constitution-on the fact that it has a jurisdiction and, at the same time, attempting, through sophistry-there is no other word for the twisted reasoning put forward by the Minister of Justice-to show that this jurisdiction must not, will not, and cannot be exercised by the federal power invested with it?

Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Justice is trying to justify this transfer by asserting that it is not a constitutional transfer of jurisdiction, but simply the entrusting of a mandate or, if you prefer, of an agency to the provincial government by the federal government.
The minister said: ""You know, Mr. Chairman, that the federal government cannot exercise its jurisdiction directly. It exercises it through its officers or other persons . . . ""; he

seems to put on the same footing ordinary civil servants or an agency of the federal government, and the government of the province of Quebec, a government which, in its own jurisdiction, is in fact and under the constitution, absolutely sovereign.

Thus, if we accept the philosophy of the Minister of Justice, we must conclude that this provincial government simply becomes a mandatary of the federal government. That is the absurdity to which we must necessarily and inevitably come, if we accept and follow the reasoning of the Minister of Justice.

It is absolutely clear that this theory is unacceptable from a constitutional point of view, because, besides the reasons I just stated, it is clear that the federal government, even under an alleged agreement or convention with the provincial government, cannot alter the jurisdictions of each level of government as definitively set out by sections 91 and 92 of the British North America Act.

The theory of the Minister of Justice is therefore absolutely groundless from a constitutional point of view. If he cannot justify his theory from a constitutional point of view, surely, he could not justify it under any piece of legislation? In that respect, the minister made a real effort.

He said that such a transfer was not new, that the government had proceeded in the same way for some services to the Indians. Either the minister neglected to consider the question carefully or he abused himself on the meaning of the transfer of services in respect to Indians. For in the latter case, it was a transfer authorized by legislation passed by this parliament, as indeed the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) pointed out to the minister during his remarks.

In this case, there is no legislation before the house providing for this transfer. What is more surprising, neither the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) nor the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) indicate that the government intends to introduce such legislation in the house.

So, their argument is fundamentally unsound, if they want to invoke legislation, for in this case there is no legislation. Nothing in the existing legislation concerning Indians provides for the transfer discussed in this debate.

The argument of the minister with respect to the constitution of this mandate is not justified either by an agreement or consent which would have been given by the people concerned themselves, that is the Eskimo people, for the Minister of Justice was again of an amazing, of an astounding
fugacity with respect to this so-called referendum. We have absolutely no assurance on the part of the government in this regard.
In view of the principles I have just put forward, I suggest that everybody, both federalists and provincialists, were disappointed in the speech made by the Minister of Justice.

In addition, I feel that this mandate theory puts the province in an inferior position that it can hardly deem acceptable. I say this, because I am quite familiar with the provisions of the civil code pertaining to mandate. As a matter of fact, a definition of a mandate is given in section 1701 and following sections of the civil code.

Thus, section 1701 defines a mandate as a contract by which a person called the mandator, commits a lawful business to the management of another, called the mandatary. Therefore, in the present case, the federal government would be the mandator and the province, the mandatary, which by accepting the mandate is obliged to execute it.
The next chapter of the civil code sets forth the obligations resulting from the mandate. Section 1709 provides among other things that:
The mandatary is obliged to execute the mandate which he has accepted.
Section 1713 provides that:
The mandatary is bound to render an account of his administration.

It follows therefore that if the province of Quebec is willing to be the mandatary of the federal government in this matter, it accepts a direct and inevitable control by the federal government in this field and agrees to account for its activities.

In other words, if the province of Quebec builds schools and sets up a curriculum, it must submit it to the central government. Can you imagine a more evident intrusion in the absolute jurisdiction of the provinces in the field of education?

This federal control in the field of education, if the argument of the Minister of Justice and that of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources is accepted, was confirmed yesterday by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources himself when he stated, among other things, as reported on page 1976 of Hansard that, for example, the federal government will require:
-the standards.. .would have to be as good as those we have now and, in addition, would have to take care of the future requirements of the population.
And in reply to a question of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) the minister repeated again that the federal government should not exercise that control in such a field.
Supply-Northern Affairs
It is for these reasons that I say the speech of the Minister of Justice has greatly disappointed all those who were expecting a little logic from him on this matter.
It is a fine thing to say that the provincial government will accept such conditions; that it will accept to be the federal government's mandatary or agent, in other words, to be its servant.
I was dismayed, yesterday, when, in reply to my question:
Has the government of the province of Quebec accepted to have conditions thus imposed by the federal government?
The Minister of Justice said:
That is my understanding under the preliminary agreement which has already been mentioned-

In view of the present state of Canadian politics, in the light of today's realities and the stand taken consistently by the successive governments of the province of Quebec and accepted today, 1 cannot see the federal government dictating conditions to the provincial government in such a vital field.

Above all, I cannot see the minister of natural resources of the province of Quebec, Mr. Rene Levesque, for instance, accepting such dictatorship-there is no other word, dictate and dictatorship are synonyms-from the federal government.

I cannot see the provincial government making such an about-face, especially since the premier of Quebec stated last week, after the failure of the federal-provincial conference in Quebec city, that his government would take legal proceedings against the federal administration to have the student loans and the family allowances legislation declared ultra vires.

I can see it even less after what we heard on the radio today-and the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Dupuis) and the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne) may be able to tell us whether it is true-that behind closed doors, the Quebec Liberal federation is putting the final touch to the final and complete divorce from the federal wing of the party.
Under the circumstances-

2272660,ca.proc.d.1964-04-10.24.10,1964-04-10,84ed4838-0481-4feb-903d-e74c47997afa,ca.m.9475,Mr. Mariineau:,,DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES,,,I am very pleased to answer the point of order raised by my hon. opposite. It is unfortunate that he was not in the house at the beginning of the sitting for he would know that I did quote the Minister of Justice from the text. If he wants further information in this regard, he could read carefully what the minister said in this connection.
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to go into details. Up to now I have only tried to underline the complete inconsistency of the attitude of the federal government in regard to the transfer of the Eskimos.

Personally, I think I have made my position clear when I participated in a debate on the same question on March 26 last. Here was the stand I took then: the transfer of the ""jurisdiction"" of the Eskimos' administrative affairs was recommended by a joint committee on Indian affairs in 1961. The matters which were proposed to be transferred came under the exclusive jurisdiction of the province. The committee recommended certain conditions under which the transfer was to be made, for instance, that the transfer be agreed upon by the Indians themselves and then ratified by the federal and provincial legislatures.
I want to say that, as far as self-determination is concerned, the Eskimos have surely some rights and that we, of the province of Quebec, would be the last ones to deny them those rights.
[Mr. Martineau.l

Mr. Chairman, I shall conclude my remarks by saying that I am convinced that should this transfer be made according to the rules I have mentioned, and in accordance with the recommendations of the joint committee of the parliament of Canada, the government of the province of Quebec, which would then exercise its authority in a field which properly belongs to it, would jealously maintain and completely safeguard the fundamental rights, the culture and the language of the Eskimos.

Mr. Chairman, that is the stand I took in the past and which I still take. That is the issue. The minister of northern affairs said yesterday that the ultimate objective of the federal government was to promote the full and complete emancipation of the Eskimos. I am all for it, if such is the real objective of the government. But then, let the government treat the Eskimos with the respect they are entitled to as intelligent human beings and not try to outsmart them. It should not be wily with them, for they are Canadian citizens.

Mr. Chairman, the government ought not to try and confuse an issue which should be absolutely clearcut. On the one hand, we have the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources telling us that the federal government is at odds with Quebec on the matter and, on the other, the Minister of Justice saying that the provincial government accepts the federal government's conditions and that they have consulted each other. He should rather tell us what is the attitude of the federal government in that respect. There cannot be as many attitudes as there are ministers. If they are unable to settle this matter, they should not endeavour to do it because, instead of finding a solution, they would be getting away from it.

Mr. Chairman, before the end of this degovernment, in dealing with this matter, must respect the Canadian constitution and the sovereignty of parliament, and above all the rights and interests of the Eskimos. Until now, they have given no evidence that they would settle the matter on the basis of standards dear to them. Well, Mr. Chairman, since Eskimos are human beings endowed with keen intelligence, as everyone knows, I feel it is shameful and entirely unthinkable to approach such a vital question that way.

Mr. Chairman, before the end of this debate, I would like the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources to answer questions directed to him yesterday by members on this side of the house. We would like him to outline the policy the government intend to follow in that respect.

,Progressive Conservative,,Paul Raymond Martineau,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=84ed4838-0481-4feb-903d-e74c47997afa&Language=E&Section=ALL
2272661,ca.proc.d.1964-04-10.24.11,1964-04-10,88de9baa-8839-401f-9aa2-55522b62d47f,ca.m.3979,Mr. Baldwin:,,DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES,,,Mr. Chairman, I will not be very long, and I make no apology for commenting on this item. I think we have before us two of the most important principles with which this parliament has yet had to deal in my memory. There are two things involved. I suggest the first is a denial of natural justice to the Eskimo people. I am not going to deal with that point very much because it has been dealt with adequately by my leader, by the hon. member for Yukon and other hon. members on this side.

It was all very well for the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources to say last night that no formal agreement has been entered into yet, but having examined Hansard, having had an opportunity to read the questions and answers with respect to this problem, having seen the statements made and having read the press reports, I suggest that no other reasonable interpretation can be placed on the situation but that the government has committed itself to enter into an agreement by which there will be placed in the hands of the government of Quebec certain responsibilities with regard to the Eskimo people. True enough, as the minister said, the fine print has not yet been completed, and I think it is to the credit of the minister that he has seen fit to hold out until he thinks there are adequate safeguards in the agreement which is to be made. However, that the government is committed is, I think, perfectly obvious.

I think we have now gone so far on this question, Mr. Chairman, that natural justice will be denied unless the Eskimo people have the opportunity to express their views by means of a referendum. I leave this aspect by quoting again a statement Sir Wilfrid Laurier made many years ago, which I quoted on March 20 in the budget debate. I think what he said with respect to the people of Quebec applies just as much now as it did then.

Yes, we are too much the sons of France, of that generous nation which has so often shed her blood for the defence of the weak, of the oppressed, not to be ever ready to defend the rights of our fellow countrymen of different nationalities to the same extent as our own.

It is my submission, and I fully believe, that the people of the province of Quebec would not wish any such transfer of responsibility to be consummated without the Eskimo people having the opportunity to express their views by a referendum.

I leave that point and will now deal very briefly with the legal aspect. I say that there has been a denial of natural justice. I add to that by saying that what is proposed to be done is that such transfers as take place will be consummated without due process of

Supply-Northern Affairs law. I posed the question on April 6, when I spoke briefly on the estimates of the Department of Justice. I spoke on purpose at that time, to give the Minister of Justice an opportunity to examine my arguments, which I feel I put before the committee dispassionately and with due regard to the facts and the law of the situation. At the conclusion of my remarks I said this:
Until parliament has given the government the right to give to a provincial government any of its responsibilities in respect of these Indians-
-that should have been Eskimos-
-then the action which the government proposes to take is completely unconstitutional and not within the purview of the government as opposed to parliament.
How did the Minister of Justice answer this question? Yesterday, as recorded at page 1966 of Hansard, he made these remarks:

Mr. Chairman, I was saying that the agreements which were and continue to be made in regard to Indian affairs are made in the framework of the exercise, by the federal government, of its administrative jurisdiction in the field of Indian affairs.

So the minister is saying at this point that we can do this so far as the Eskimos are concerned because in the past we have done it in respect to the Indians. Further down the page he is recorded as saying:

And in the same way that no one can question our right to deal with Eskimo affairs through agents, representatives, intermediaries... I do not see why, so long as the decision quoted by the Leader of the Opposition is not against that and that there is no transfer of jurisdiction, we could not use, in the same way, a provincial government to manage Eskimo affairs-

I see, Mr. Chairman, that the Minister of Transport is in the house. At one time he was minister of citizenship and immigration and, as such, had jurisdiction over Indian affairs. I am sure he will bear me out that with respect to Indians, as interpreted and defined in the Indian Act, the act constitutes a complete code, and in that act there are a number of sections by which parliament, having first had an opportunity to debate this issue, having first had an opportunity to express its view, having first in committee of the whole examined clause by clause the provisions of the Indian Act saw fit-and I think properly-to entrust to the government the right by order in council to regulate, to make agreements, and to give in particular to the provincial governments and to local school boards certain agreements with respect to education and other matters.
It is only because parliament, being supreme to do so, delegated its authority to the government that the government has the
Supply-Northern Affairs right, and has exercised that right on a number of occasions, to enter into agreements with the provincial governments.

,Progressive Conservative,,Gerald William Baldwin,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=88de9baa-8839-401f-9aa2-55522b62d47f&Language=E&Section=ALL
2272662,ca.proc.d.1964-04-10.24.12,1964-04-10,5996b081-97f6-4bde-8dec-52df3dca3f76,ca.m.9560,Mr. Pickersgill:,Minister of Transport,DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES,,,I wonder if the hon. gentleman, having brought me into this, would answer this question. The hon. gentleman is quite right that under the Indian Act the government was entrusted with the power, the faculty, of making these agreements. In fact I made many of them. I made an over-all agreement with the Northwest Territories council no different in many respects from what is proposed in this case.

But I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if it is not true either that Eskimos are Indians, and therefore they are covered by the provisions of that act or, if they are not Indians, they are just ordinary Canadian citizens and therefore should be treated as ordinary Canadian citizens? It seems to me they must be one or the other. They are not some third thing. They are either Indians, and therefore covered by the Indian Act, and the minister in charge of Indian affairs has the right to make an agreement as he did with other Indians; or they are not Indians and, if they are not Indians, then they are just ordinary Canadian citizens.

,Liberal,,John Whitney Pickersgill,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=5996b081-97f6-4bde-8dec-52df3dca3f76&Language=E&Section=ALL
2272665,ca.proc.d.1964-04-10.24.15,1964-04-10,88de9baa-8839-401f-9aa2-55522b62d47f,ca.m.3979,Mr. Baldwin:,,DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES,,,They are a third body. Under section 4 of the Indian Act, Eskimos are specifically excluded from the operation of that act. Consequently they are not covered by the provisions of that act, and there cannot be valid agreements made by the government in the same way as agreements can be made by the government with respect to Indians. But equally they are not ordinary citizens in the same sense, because by the supreme court case the parliament of Canada has been invested with exclusive jurisdiction and responsibility.

For that reason, because of this anomaly which may not have occurred to people before but which definitely exists, the Eskimos in northern Quebec covered by the supreme court case are the exclusive responsibility of the federal government, and they cannot be included within the four corners of the Indian Act.

I have dealt with the question of the estimates, and I should like to conclude by stating what I think are the four safeguards that should be provided before any agreement is entered into. Let me say that I sat on the Indian affairs joint committee, and it is my considered opinion that in the final analysis and in due course it is desirable that distinctions between citizens in Canada should be eliminated; but let me also say that because of the manner in which this particular issue has been handled it is my view that the government has set back the process of adjustment by at least a generation.

I make these suggestions; first, that any agreement which is to be made must be submitted to parliament and must have parliamentary approval. Second, there should be adequate safeguards in this agreement; third, a safeguard of arbitration by means of reference to possibly a supreme court judge or the Supreme Court of Canada should the Eskimo people feel that the provisions for protecting them are being violated; fourth, there can only be settlement now after a referendum.

2272726,ca.proc.d.1964-04-10.24.76,1964-04-10,451d41d6-6f60-40ef-87f1-bd1aea75e8c2,ca.m.1579,Mr. Peters:,,DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES,,,Mr. Chairman, I do not want to get involved in the discussion which has taken place, but it seems to me that the remarks which have been made are a pretty good indication that there is some agreement as to what are the legal requirements. While I cannot see why Eskimos and Indians are put in the same category, there is probably a legal reason for so doing. However, why is the province of Quebec so interested in reaching an agreement that the federal government should give up its control over the Eskimo population in this particular area?

One question which is asked, and I think it is a good question, is, is this because of the squatters' rights that the Eskimos obviously have in regard to the natural resources in what is called New Quebec? Has this also something to do with the boundary between Labrador and Quebec in relation to the local inhabitants of the area? Is that why the people of Quebec are so interested in them, and particularly the government of Quebec, because there is certainly a distinction between the two which we should draw. For example, Mr. Levesque is interested in obtaining this concession from the federal government, even though it has been said that he still wants some of the administration costs to be paid by this government

The rest of us in Canada have two responsibilities in this regard. One of them is to see that the people who are our native population, whether they be called Indians or Eskimos, have their rights protected. If we are willing to send our troops into other nations across the world to protect their right to self-determination, then at least we should be able to apply this principle in our relationships between the federal government and the provincial governments of Canada. This is very fundamental, and any member of parliament who comes here unprepared to meet this commitment on behalf of the native population of this country is doing a great disservice to the people of Canada and to the idea of a united Canadian nation.

It is my opinion that many of these people have reached the stage where they can achieve self-determination. From talking to people who have visited the Eskimos in some communities I believe that the Eskimos have already made this decision, and the only thing preventing the implementation is that they want to retain their preferred position under the control of the federal government, and have an outspoken objection to being
transferred to the control of the province in which they may reside. They believe they have certain advantages in remaining under the control and responsibility of the federal government.

I do not think we as Canadians are the least bit interested in whether a province wishes to obtain clear title to a particular area in this regard. This should not concern us at all. What should concern us is the welfare of these people. It seems to me very surprising that this government should insist upon us making this decision without taking into consideration the wishes of the people in those areas.

I can only conclude, Mr. Chairman, as many others have concluded, that when all the smoke dies down and the legal precedents have been cited, we will find this whole matter hinges upon the commitment the Liberal government in Ottawa made to the Liberal government in Quebec. I feel it is as simple as that. This problem did not come to the fore until there had been a meeting of the resource minister of Quebec with the minister of northern affairs for Canada.

I had an opportunity some time ago, along with other members of parliament, of seeing a film outlining some of these problems. This film was paid for by certain interests in the province of Quebec and illustrated the conditions under which the Eskimos existed in the Arctic region. The particular gentleman who took the film went up to the Arctic and set up a trading company in that area. This film showed great abuses by employees of northern affairs who worked in that area, particularly where there was a relationship between the Hudson's Bay Company and the department of northern affairs. One example concerned oil declared surplus by the Department of National Defence which was turned over to the Hudson's Bay Company. This oil was not suitable for outboard motors. However, the Hudson's Bay factors would not stock any outboard motor oil on their shelves until this surplus oil had been used up.

This incident was brought to the attention of the department of northern affairs, but nothing was done about it. There were other illustrations. The post office was run by the Hudson's Bay Company, and people in the area could not obtain cash unless this was done through the auspices of the Hudson's Bay Company. This was done on a very discriminatory basis. The gentleman who came back had in his suit coat a number of packages containing bills of large denominations which he had been using while in the Arctic because he was not permitted to have cheques cashed in that area.
Supply-Northern Affairs

As I have said, Mr. Chairman, all these incidents came to the attention of the department of northern affairs. Representatives of that department viewed this film and made very disparaging remarks while the film was being shown. They showed great ignorance in doing so. In view of the fact that this film was being shown to us by the film board in their quarters, these people could have shown courtesy to the other guests who wanted to listen. I am sure these matters must have been discussed within the department. I was interested in ascertaining why certain individuals in Quebec would pay to support such an expedition to obtain this type of film. Since discussing the matter with a number of other people, I am satisfied the reason it was done was that the province of Quebec had already decided they wanted to get control of the Indian population in that area. It was simply a case of squatters rights in connection with the resources that existed in this area.

If this is true, and I believe it to be true, then I believe these Eskimos should be given the same protection that is afforded by the Indian Act. We are all well aware of the fact that if this area were declared to be a reservation for Indian bands, then the resources of the area could be developed for the benefit of the people of the area. I am quite sure, Mr. Chairman, that one major mining company in northern Quebec would more than support in perpetuity the 2,300 Eskimos in that area. In all fairness, if the minister really wishes to protect these people he is going to have to give a much clearer indication of this desire than he has in the past. He will have to allow the Eskimos to determine their own future.

There are other problems which I believe will arise before the committee can give approval to the recommendations outlined in the memorandum the minister presented to parliament. There are matters such as religion, education, language and so on, that will be of concern to the Eskimo people in the future. We must insist that the minister not proceed further with these negotiations with Quebec, Manitoba or the other provinces until the very fundamental problem of the responsibility for these people be established throughout the whole area.

I wish to refer to one or two other matters which have been raised in this house, Mr. Chairman, and I am sorry the Minister of Justice is not here to listen; because I want to show just what type of deviousness has been exercised by the ministers on the treasury benches when dealing with this question.

For some 20 or 25 minutes yesterday the Minister of Justice skirted all around the points raised and did not answer directly one single proposition put to him by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition and other members on this side who dealt with the constitutional issues. I said to the minister, when I was speaking, that he had mentioned a draft agreement. He said he had mentioned no such draft agreement in his remarks, and I said that Hansard would show that he did just that. I said to the minister that no amount of wriggling could get away from those words in Hansard. I want to read them now that Hansard for yesterday has been printed. His words will be found on page 1965, in the left hand column. The minister said this:

But what happens in the same case? It has been decided that nothing prevents the federal government, in the exercise of its own jurisdiction, from selecting a body of the provincial government as its representative, its agent to exercise, in accordance with conditions laid down by the federal government, a federal jurisdiction; and the fact that this agent acts on behalf of the federal government is not unlawful, but on the contrary it is completely in accordance with the constitution-

What, then, is the matter involved here? It is merely for the moment a draft agreement under which the Quebec government would agree to look after the administration of Eskimo affairs in the far north, on behalf of the federal government.
They were the minister's words, and within half an hour he denied ever having uttered them.

Again on the same page, six or eight lines from the bottom of the left hand column, he referred to a draft agreement. When I put this question directly to the Minister of Justice and challenged him to deny the existence of a draft agreement, the minister of northern affairs intervened, and as reported at page 1969 he made this observation:
Mr. Chairman, I think the Minister of Justice has no reason to have any such knowledge of the matter at all;

What is more ridiculous than for the minister of northern affairs to say that the Minister of Justice, who has been in on consultations with the Quebec government officials, has no reason to have any knowledge of the matter at all?

I believe, Mr. Chairman, that the government is hiding something. I believe we are entitled to an explanation as to the underlying reasons for this continued evasiveness. The minister has been sitting in his seat throughout this debate and has said nothing substantial whatever in reply to the questions which have been put to him. He has been asked questions by the hon. member for Vancouver East, the hon. member for Skeena, the hon. member for Timiskaming, as well as several hon. members from this party. Not one of those questions has he answered. He did answer one of mine, and I will accept his word for it, although he cannot blame me for being suspicious at his assertion that there is no agreement in existence. But I am suggesting to him that he has to go further than that. I am suggesting to him that he has to tell us how far these negotiations, so-called, have gone with the Quebec government officials. He must also tell us what is the underlying reason for his colleagues and the government transferring jurisdiction.

The Minister of Justice makes a great show of saying that all the government is doing is transferring the administrative control to the provincial authorities. Surely when administrative control is transferred one cannot get out from under the fact that with that transfer of administrative control must of necessity go a transfer of the power to make policy decisions. Let us assume for a moment that administrative control does pass. Surely with that administrative control is going to go the power to make decisions as to the curricula to be taught in schools; as to the standard of health to be maintained; as to whether welfare programs will be applicable. All these are matters of policy, and you cannot say under the blanket of a smokescreen that we are retaining on behalf of the federal government this responsibility and merely transferring the paper work to the province of Quebec. That matter has to be
clarified before the hon. members of this house should be asked to accept any such transfer.

The Minister of Transport in his intervention when the hon. member for Peace River was speaking, which intervention I suggest served more to confuse than to add anything, asked a question concerning the Eskimo people of Manitoba. This too has no relation to the problem at all because there were no Eskimos in Manitoba, as the minister well knows. The federal government transported them from the Northwest Territories into the province. If he is using that as the basis of his argument he might as well say that the federal government could transfer all the Eskimo people from their homes in the north to Prince Edward Island and transfer jurisdiction over them to that province. So that the minister's argument on that point is specious indeed.

Another very important question which the minister must answer before this item passes relates to the dismissal of Mr. Mc-Taggart. The minister rose in the house when asked a question on the matter the other day and stated that Mr. McTaggart did not resign, but Mr. McTaggart himself seems to have another view. In an article appearing in the Winnipeg Free Press Mr. McTaggart is quoted as having said that the Quebec authorities-
-have been carrying on a ""smear campaign"" aimed at ""getting rid of anybody who has any influence on the Quebec Eskimos"".
The article continues:
He said that Mr. Laing, on his visit to Fort Chimo, was told by Eskimo leaders that they did not want their affairs to be taken over by the provincial government.

Mr. McTaggart went on to say, after having explained how he published certain of his views in the Northern Star, which is a mimeographed newspaper which he started three years ago in order to knit the Eskimo community of Fort Chimo together, that:
Within a day, word of the article had reached Ottawa and a rocket was heading back to Mr. McTaggart telling him to keep quiet.
It came in the form of a letter from the director of the northern administration branch of the department of northern affairs to the department's acting administrator in Fort Chimo.
The letter pointed out that department regulations prohibit federal employees from writing for publications on department matters without prior clearance from their superiors.
It closed with these words:-
This is the letter from the department as reported in the Winnipeg Free Press:
In no way whatsoever am I anxious to take any action which could be construed as curtailing the freedom of the press, but at the moment it is
Supply-Northern Affairs
almost imprudent for any departmental employee to publish unauthorized articles on the subject of Eskimo affairs in northern Quebec"".

If it was not the intention to limit the expression of free speech, why did the directive not include a specification that there be no opinions published at all without clearing them through the department? Why restrict it to this one problem? Why was he told to be silent only with regard to the Eskimos of northern Quebec? I think there is some explanation required there. The letter continues:

Mr. McTaggart is, therefore, asked to govern himself accordingly and to publish nothing on this subject or any other matter of departmental business without first obtaining approval from the district administrator"".
At the moment, Mr. McTaggart said, that appeared to be the end of it and he prepared to comply with the directive.
A few days later, he received another letter telling him that, since he had broken the directive, he was being transferred immediately out of Fort Chimo. He was told to be out by March 6.

This man was the principal of a school who had occupied that office for three and a half years and was prepared to comply with the directive issued by the minister's department. A few days after receiving this letter-unless there was some intervening conduct of which the members of this committee have not been told-having done nothing further to raise the ire of the departmental officials, he is told to be out by March 6. Why? Was he a disturbing influence on the relations which the government wanted to maintain with the government of which Mr. Levesque is a member? I think some explanation should be forthcoming there.

Mr. McTaggart spent a week in Ottawa and was offered another school in the Northwest Territories. Instead, he turned in his resignation. What other course was there for this gentleman to follow? The department practically said ""Get out of the school at Fort Chimo where you have been principal for three and a half years, in the middle of the term, and here is another school."" This was in the middle of the winter, and he was tossed out on his ear by the department. The other teachers followed by requesting transfers out of Quebec.

Now, I think we are entitled to explanations today. There seems to be a certain amount of loyalty expressed by the teachers at Fort Chimo school for the actions of Mr. McTaggart, even though they did not appear to be consistent with what the government wanted. When he was asked by the interviewer, probably the gentleman who wrote the article, why he was transferred when the matter had apparently been settled by a warning, Mr. McTaggart said ""I'm told it
Supply-Northern Affairs was pressure from Rene Levesque's department."" This was Mr. McTaggart's answer.
Now, these questions have to be answered. The minister cannot discharge his responsibility to this committee by remaining silent any longer. Someone

This area is a part of the province of Quebec, and the government of that province are anxious to extend development of their province northward. We know that, among other things, a very important deposit of asbestos has been found at Sugluk, which is on the northwest corner of the extended great peninsula. There have also been other indications. A number of iron deposits have been found and there are other minerals there. The province is looking forward, of course, to the development of the northern part of its territory.

This situation has existed throughout the term of the present government and also the previous government so far as the citizens there are concerned. After all, people are the first asset of the region, and unless you can use the people who are there you are not going to develop the resources that lie there. The citizens are Eskimos whose numbers are added to by a small number of white persons who, almost without exception, have been employees of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. I have given figures such as 250 Eskimos and seven white people. The seven white people are employees of ours. I believe these are the reasons the government of Quebec is interested.

With regard to the innuendo that has been thrown at me and the manufactured questions and half-manufactured answers of the hon. member for Vancouver East and the hon. member for Yukon, I can only say that I stated the actual facts yesterday and if hon. members will read what I said then, they will see what the situation is. 2272821,ca.proc.d.1964-04-10.24.171,1964-04-10,355fae5e-9d52-46cc-a5dd-2658a81a0ea7,ca.m.5197,Mr. Laing:,Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources,DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES,,,The matter of the constitutional responsibility of the various provinces with respect to these people has been dealt with by the Minister of Justice and other members of the house, and I am not going to deal with it. I think it has been agreed in all corners of the house that in the years that lie ahead of us the best results with respect to these indigenous peoples will be achieved by bringing them into general comity with the other people resident in the areas where they live. If members on the other side are going to say this is not the year to do it in Quebec, that is another matter, but generally speaking I think there is universal agreement that this is the best thing for all concerned.

Instances can be given of agreements made when the right hon. gentleman was in power with respect to education in a number of places in Canada, and I can assure him that the results have been excellent indeed. We have 2,300 Indian children in our high schools in the province of British Columbia today, and I want to say that they are as good students as any others. I think that policy would meet with the approval of members on both sides of the house. But if it is going to be contended in respect of the Eskimos of northern Quebec that this is not the time, that is another matter; and that argument can be made, of course, in respect of any area or group of people in Canada from time to time.

2272961,ca.proc.d.1964-04-10.27.12,1964-04-10,ba1f4916-0b63-4654-9f27-242c3d276e6e,ca.m.6904,Mr. Howard:,,PRIVY COUNCIL,,,"Before we proceed to pass this vote, inasmuch as it involves the royal commission on bilingualism and biculturalism I should like to make a few brief comments about that commission and about its origins, and perhaps express some regrets as to the course followed so far in this particular field.

I think all of us as we look back will recall that this royal commission had its founding days when the present Prime Minister sat on this side of the house as leader of the opposition and when he was, I would say, desperately groping for some appealing things to say, rather than looking in depth at the question of the culture and linguistic structure of Canada. I think what happened really was that he stumbled on to the thought of a royal commission on bilingualism without any great thought about it, found it was appealing and so was sort of stuck with it.

In the initial instance, I think without his thinking too clearly about it the present Prime Minister when he was over here as leader of the opposition looked on this as being something which would be appealing to one particular province of Canada rather than as something which might be of benefit and help to all of Canada, and the impression which was received by many people in Canada was that it was a commission slanted in one direction, orientated to one theme or designed to appeal to one group of people in Canada.

It is unfortunate that this happened. I think that if the Prime Minister and his government had done some public relations work and prepared the people in the western part of Canada, as I know them, and in the

east, and in the east in the maritimes, as it has been related to me-if they had prepared people in those areas for the acceptance of the idea of such a commission, it would have been more readily accepted and appreciated as something which might be beneficial to the whole recognition of the culture of Canada.

I might recall the immediate reaction of the premier of Alberta to this royal commission, a reaction which gives some indication of the attitude the people in the west had about it. In one sense, and I do not want to say this by way of derogation, the very terms of that royal commission are an insult to one group of people in Canada-the one we have been discussing for some days now. I refer particularly to the original inhabitants of this nation, those whom we now classify as Indian and Eskimo people. If we are going to have a commission to inquire into the cultural aspects of the people of Canada, surely our Indian people should have been placed in the forefront of any consideration, rather than being relegated, as they are in the commission's terms of reference, to one of the other ethnic groups.

The terms of reference have been referred to many times and they are pretty well confined within the first paragraph of the order in council setting up the commission, which gives them the authority ""to inquire into and report""-I am reading now from the terms of reference-""upon the existing state of bilingualism and biculturalism in Canada and to recommend what steps should be taken to develop the Canadian confederation on the basis of an equal partnership between the two founding races, taking into account the contribution made by the other ethnic groups to the cultural enrichment of Canada and the measures that should be taken to safeguard that contribution."" It is the reference to ""other ethnic groups"", among them being the original inhabitants of Canada that I say is a somewhat insulting approach.

In addition to that, the commission is charged with the responsibility of recommending what steps should be taken to develop the Canadian confederation on the basis of an equal partnership between the two founding races. Again, this is completely disregarding the fact that our native Indian and Eskimo population, as we call them now, were the very peoples who founded or participated in the founding of Canada. There must be prime concern given to the culture and history of these people if we are to have any real understanding of what comprises Canada. It is true, I think, that we can inquire into the state of bilingualism, as the commission is charged to do, but I doubt very much whether we can inquire into the state of biculturalism, because

such a thing does not exist and, I submit, cannot exist. We cannot have a ""bi"" or ""tri"" or ""quadri"" or any other kind of multiple culture. You have a culture, and it is not divisible. That is what people participate in. For the sake of argument, I can never become a part of the culture of the people of French parentage who were born and raised in the province of Quebec. I cannot do that because I was not born in that environment and of that parentage. Conversely, neither can anyone else have the culture, in the full sense of the word, of any other citizen or any other person unless he was born into that environment and followed a particular national lineage in his inheritance. To my mind it is rather an anomaly to ask a group of people to inquire into the state of biculturalism.

Marcel Chaput's book entitled ""Why I am a separatist"" makes reference to this perhaps, in a way, when he refers to bilingualism, although in reading the preliminary part of it he is in fact using the language as a part of culture. He says this:

There isn't a single bilingual people in the world, not even the Belgians or the Swiss. Bilingualism is a meaningless word, a sin against nature. At most, there are nations made up of several unilingual groups joined under a common government, such as Belgium and Switzerland.
The reason is simple-a man can only have one pattern of thought.
Here he refers to the question of a culture:

He is like a tree whose branches all spring from the one trunk. His knowledge of a second language must take the form of an offshoot from his native language. But in our case, bilingualism is nothing more than a pernicious union of two branches, with no trunk at all, which can only result in a stunted and deformed knowledge of our native language.

He is referring particularly there, of course, to the French language; but I submit that in a sense taking those words in the broad sense and referring them to culture in the true sense of the word, it is ridiculous to appoint a royal commission to inquire into the state of biculturalism when no such state or condition can possibly exist. There is only a culture, as I said earlier, and one cannot have the culture of another; he can only come to the point of respecting and admiring the culture of another and hoping that mutual respect and admiration is generated thereby. Perhaps in the light especially of the recently concluded-or perhaps it was adjourned-federal-provincial conference in Quebec we should go a bit further afield and wonder just what is to be the relationship in this country between those who acclaim one inheritance and those who acclaim another. I think it becomes obvious more and more as each day goes by, more and more as each federal-provincial conference is held,

Supply-Privy Council more and more as each question arises over which there might be dual jurisdiction, that the demands-not the demands of Quebec, but the position of Quebec-of Premier Le-sage are for some peculiar political reason almost insatiable. The Canadian government will find itself giving in, time and time and time again to these incessant demands of the premier of that province and of others in his cabinet. Some of us have studied or have read about the effect that narcotic drugs have upon an individual. Progressively, if he cannot get enough his demand increases. He starts off with a little bit and continually day after day, demands more and more and more and greater dosages of the narcotic drug in order to maintain a particular state. This is the condition that exists in the government of Quebec; it is something similar to that of a drug addict.

Normally and in the initial instance there were many people who came from the extremes of east and west Canada who, not having grown up in the environment of and with the history or the knowledge in any intimate way of the history of Quebec and what took place there, had an attitude of great sympathy toward people in Quebec who claimed they had been wronged. There was a desire to understand and work with those who claimed that wrongs had been committed against them, and to right and correct those wrongs. I know this was the situation at home amongst people whom I know, people who were born and raised on the west coast who really did not have any great involvement with people living in central Canada 3,000 miles away, except by way of reading in the newspapers, watching the television newscasts or listening to radio broadcasts, or something like that, and who initially were desirous of wanting to find a solution to what was claimed to be a wrongdoing in the first instance.
Unfortunately this feeling is developing into a resentment; it is developing into a resentment because, as I said, the demands are becoming more and more insatiable all the time.

I think it is time to think not in terms of retaliating, which is what some people are talking about, but to think in terms of accepting the fact that we might as well proceed on the assumption that we are going to have a Canada consisting of nine provinces, and that Quebec will be a separate entity within the geographic area and will fit into the picture in as loose a way as Quebec wants. This is something which the government has not accepted. It is something which the Prime Minister, master diplomat that he is, cannot accept, probably because of his background

Supply-Privy Council activity in the field of diplomacy and external affairs, which consists of attempting to listen to different sides of the question and to smooth things over as much as possible. But this is not possible with the province of Quebec, and the sooner we accept that fact and that we can develop and work together to build a Canadian confederation as I have just indicated, the better off we will be, and the better off they will be in Quebec.

If we do not follow that course the government of Canada, no matter who happens to form it, will find itself saying to Quebec: ""Yes, we will give you 35 per cent of the tax revenue"". The next day it will say: ""Yes, we will give you everything by way of succession duty taxes"". Then the next day it will say: ""Yes, you can opt out of the hospital insurance program and we will pay you more"". As a result we will find out that what will happen will be that Canada will give and give and give until there is nothing left to give. The result will be that the Canadian nation will collapse and no sort of reasonably amicable relationship will exist in the country. But I submit that if we take the other course of accepting the fact that Quebec's demands are insatiable and cannot be met from the pockets of the rest of the people of Canada, the sooner we will be able to go on and build something worth while.

,New Democratic Party,,Frank Howard,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=ba1f4916-0b63-4654-9f27-242c3d276e6e&Language=E&Section=ALL
2272962,ca.proc.d.1964-04-10.27.13,1964-04-10,af0c867e-b570-40f2-b26a-5d005e6d5a98,ca.m.3027,Mr. Olson:,,PRIVY COUNCIL,,,Mr. Chairman, just one or two remarks on this item. First of all, we have spent $275,850 on the royal commission on biculturalism and bilingualism, and I presume this amount has been spent on the commission up to the end of March of 1964. I should like to ask the President of the Privy Council whether that is the case, and I should like some detail as to what the money has been spent on.

My second point is this. During the course of questions on the orders of the day and in various other debates the Prime Minister and other front benchers on the government side have repeatedly admonished some members of the opposition to speak of those things which unite Canada rather than those which divide Canada. I agree that this is where the emphasis should be. I do not have before me actual quotations from the Prime Minister, but I am sure all hon. members recall occasions when he has suggested to members of the opposition that some of the statements they have made did not do anything to unite Canada, and that they would have been better left unsaid. If this amount of $275,850 is to permit the chairman and co-chairman of this commission to go about the country saying some of the things they have been saying, then I think this item should be reduced to $1.

I say that, Mr. Chairman, because in today's Globe and Mail and on the front page of today's Montreal Gazette we find expressions by the chairman and co-chairman of the commission to the effect that a parochial or provincial view is going to divide Canada and perhaps lead to her collapse. The headline to the fourth section of the Toronto Globe and Mail is this:
Provincialism could bring Canada's collapse with no one feeling at fault: Laurendeau.
Then in a report of their meeting in Toronto yesterday it is said:
Both reported that the functions of their commission had been widely misunderstood.

If that is true, I think these gentlemen should spend some time getting the people of Canada in all parts of the country to understand what is their function and what are their ultimate objectives, and how they intend to reach their aim.
I should like to make one other reference to this article, a statement attributed to Mr. Laurendeau. He is reported as saying:

French speaking citizens feared the commission would foist English upon them; English speaking Canadians, Mr. Laurendeau said, took the stand that ""if those damn French would speak English like everybody else, the problem would be solved"".

I suggest that it is precisely this sort of misinterpretation of the attitude of people in many parts of the country which is widening the division between the cultural groups of the nation. If this parliament is allowing public funds to be used so that these gentlemen can go about the country making this sort of statement, it is time the government took another look at the personalities of the chairman and co-chairman of this bilingualism and biculturalism commission and informed them that it is not their purpose to make this kind of statement, or alternatively to replace these gentlemen. I agree with the Prime Minister and with many other moderate and reasonable members of the house that we could far better spend our time emphasizing the matters which unite all of us, of whatever language or cultural group, and I suggest that perhaps we should start by saying to the people who have been appointed by this government to improve relationships that they are under the same obligation to seek those things which unite us, rather than to make ridiculous and inflammatory statements such as I have referred to in this article.

,Social Credit,,Horace Andrew (Bud) Olson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=af0c867e-b570-40f2-b26a-5d005e6d5a98&Language=E&Section=ALL
2272963,ca.proc.d.1964-04-10.27.14,1964-04-10,84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089,ca.m.3212,Mr. Diefenbaker:,Leader of the Official Opposition,PRIVY COUNCIL,,,Mr. Chairman, I have very little to say on this matter, except that we should have rather full detail from the President of the Privy Council on this very large item of $275,000 which represents, as

the hon. member for Skeena said, the expenditure up to the end of the last fiscal year. This is a large amount in respect to which we are entitled to reasonable detail. I am one of those who took the stand that a royal commission on this subject would not be beneficial to national unity. I took that stand officially in February 1963. My feeling was that it was not a royal commission which was necessary, and instead I endeavoured to bring about the convening of a national meeting of federal and provincial representatives, a meeting not of two or three days duration but a period of weeks and months, and behind closed doors. At such a meeting, men and women could discuss frankly and freely what they believe could be done by the federal and provincial governments, and we would arrive at a general agreement as to what might be done in order to assure unity within our country.

On that occasion I mentioned the question of national symbols. I mentioned the repatriation of our constitution, something we endeavoured throughout the years to achieve while I was prime minister, but without success. We are the only country within the commonwealth of nations which cannot amend its own constitution. It is ridiculous that we should be placed in a subservient position and that every time we want to amend our constitution we must go to Westminster. Certainly the British parliament does not want this vestige of the past retained. We have not attained that maturity of mind that would permit even the return to our own country of the right to amend our constitution in the parliament of Canada.

We tried for months. We met together. We found that there were objections by certain provinces and the result is that, while a royal commission studies this subject we, as a nation, still have not the right to amend our own constitution because of our failure to agree on a matter as simple as that. My view was that a royal commission could achieve nothing but the opportunity for those who are irrational and intolerant, who have a regard for this nation that is not generally held, to place their views before this commission. There are those who have some regard for the constitution of our country. Today we have a hodgepodge developing by reason of this commission being set up which is bringing about in our country a feeling that the hopes of the fathers of confederation cannot be achieved.

We need a little more faith. We need people to speak for Canada, to speak for this nation, rather than to speak for their own purposes. I am one of those who believe we can achieve unity. I think that message must be given to the Canadian people. I find in every part of

Supply-Privy Council Canada today a fear about the future of the country and its destiny. This fear has been engendered as a result of statements that are made that ought not to be made by those who have regard for the tremendous heritage that is ours, and the great destiny that will be ours if we but realize that there are two sides to every question, but that in a community of counsel we will bring about unity within the nation.

I do not want to be critical but I do agree with the hon. member for Medicine Hat. I cannot understand the concept of a royal commission which, while it takes evidence and hears representations, has periodic interpretations made by the chairmen of that commission. I do not understand this. They are supposed to be listening to the views of Canadians. They go across the country. They make speeches everywhere and they interpret their powers and their authority. I think that in doing that they are doing the greatest disservice to Canada and to the cause of unity and, above all, to the achievement of that relationship within our nation without which we cannot attain the greatness which our resources make possible. I think that a word might be spoken to these men.

This has become a commission of peripatetic after-dinner speakers who, wherever they go, interpret what they have heard in the intervening days since the last speech or the last press conference. This is not the purpose for which the commission was set up. This is not the purpose for which the Canadian people have already paid $275,000. This is not a circus parade where, in order to gratify whatever the purpose may be, the performers make speeches wherever they go. Their purpose is to endeavour, out of a diversity of viewpoint, to achieve a common degree of acceptance of principles which will enable the governments to act. After all, when the commission is through, then the work begins.

It is said the commission will continue until 1968, I believe. If we have to endure all the speeches in the next few years that we have in the last few weeks, then indeed that commission is for an unusual purpose and the commissioners are discharging their responsibilities in an unusual manner. The commission was established to try to get a consensus of viewpoint. It was not set up to interpret to the Canadian people, weekly, bi-weekly or monthly, the views of the commission. The commission started off by these commissioners announcing their views before the commission actually sat. It is not their views for which we are asking. They seem to think they speak as a body, ex cathedra to the Canadian people.
If I understand what the government had in mind when setting up the commission, the

Supply-Privy Council commission was supposed to listen to representations and finally recommend, not to make interim and interlocutory statements whenever the spirit moves them. I am not saying my idea was right, and it represented not a consensus, but my idea. It was that we would bring the provinces and federal representatives together in a national meeting. After all, the responsibility will finally rest on these two levels of government. The Prime Minister thought otherwise. The Liberal party went through the campaign undertaking to set up this commission. I want this commission, now that it is set up, to do an effective and efficient job for Canada. I do not believe it can if it continues to have chairmen as loquacious as they have been in recent days and in recent weeks.

I read the joint speeches that were made at the Empire club in the city of Toronto. I am not going to discuss the details of them, but under the circumstances I found those speeches quite beyond understanding. I say no more at this time but I do hope that the chairmen, Mr. Dunton and Mr. Lauren-deau, will come to a realization that Canadians are not interested in their periodic declarations and views but rather are interested in having this commission work effectively. I did not think it would work and I said so. It was not a popular view when I took that stand. Now that the commission has been set up I want it to succeed, but I doubt that it can unless the members of the commission begin to realize that they are not and were not appointed to be the teachers of Canadians in these difficult and trying times.

,Progressive Conservative,,John George Diefenbaker,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089&Language=E&Section=ALL
