2272980,ca.proc.d.1964-04-10.27.31,1964-04-10,6ef85d82-0243-4e17-a3bd-41a064680fd1,ca.m.4539,Mr. Gauthier:,,PRIVY COUNCIL,,,Mr. Chairman, I understand the minister has offered to give us details on item 43e and it is precisely what interests me, because I consider that $275,850 is quite a fabulous amount for an investigation which is just getting under way. I wonder what the total expenditures will be once it is completed.
I think that the chief investigators are over paid. Those people already draw a

Supply-Privy Council salary, sometimes two and even three. They are paid $100 a day and, after all, it is only a nationalistic movement. It seems to me it would have been wiser to think it over at the start, and I am asking the minister to check the expenditures because I think there is not enough control over them. It may be that another commission will have to be set up to investigate the expenditures of the royal commission on bilingualism and bicul-turalism because at this rate, the investigation will turn out to be a gold mine for some people who were appointed-I am not saying for political reasons because I have confidence in their skill-by the party in office to hold that investigation.

Now, it remains to be seen whether that investigation will give positive or negative results. Only the future will tell. I think the commissioners should have carried out an investigation instead of daily airing their own views on the report they should present to parliament. On this point, I think that I agree with the views stated by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) and the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) to the effect that if the commissioners were concerned only with their work, without making comments every day in newspapers or on the air, if they knuckled down to work without assessing their own accomplishments, I think that there would be less misunderstanding. By following such a course, the commissioners would reach the goal set for them by this government and I cannot conceive that one of the joint chairmen should pass judgment at any given moment in this way, more particularly as we know his socialistic ideas.

I think that this is a most dangerous attitude and I ask the minister to put a stop to this and ask that gentleman to do his job without foretelling the business of parliament, because, when the results are known of the inquiry we shall discuss them, and it will be up to parliament to reach a decision.

I realize that frictions which arise are always due to entirely needless balderdash on the part of one of the joint chairmen of the inquiry commission on biculturalism. The aims of that investigation are laudable in themselves, as everybody will admit. It is an ideal opportunity of getting some understanding and benefit from confederation by finding out where we stand after 97 years. At the same time, the inquiry enables us to know which province has most, or least, observed the spirit of confederation.

The objectives of the inquiry are praiseworthy if they are meant to help improving confederation. Today, there is some talk of destroying it and building up another. Let us first begin by considering the possibilities
of improving what is already built up. I think that this is the aim of the legislators who initiated the inquiry.

Now, what did the inquiry produce to date? It did enable us to find out the good and the bad sides of the matter. We had a sample of it this afternoon when listening to the remarks of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard).

It enabled a few to make their views known. At the same time it also enabled the Canadian people and the house to realize that Quebec is not the only province where there are separatists; they are much more numerous in western Canada.

Even though it would have but one result, that of eliciting statements from people who generally act without speaking, I think that it would be something worth while and that the inquiry into bilingualism and biculturalism would be fruitful. In fact, Mr. Chairman, there is nothing worse than a fellow who never says a word and who always works in the dark.

The statements that were made this afternoon prompted members from certain parties to come out of their cage and I ask those members to come and repeat in the province of Quebec the speeches they delivered in this house this afternoon. They will then be able to observe the reaction of the people from Quebec.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to be prejudiced. I am not one of those who claims that there are no French Canadians outside Quebec. Indeed not. French Canadians can be found throughout Canada. We should not forget when speaking about French Canadians, that we are referring to the entire country. As stated by the hon. member for Skeena this afternoon, people in the west say: ""But we did not know the province of Quebec before."" If they do not venture outside their own bailiwick and are like rats in a cage, we are not to blame. The citizens of Quebec are better informed about the various races that make up Canada.

The statements made this afternoon will result in a tightening of the bonds between serious-minded members who still wish to save confederation; they have awakened and realized that some provinces are still more dangerous than Quebec within confederation. This is not due to ill will but it is due to the fact that these Canadian citizens do not know Canada well enough.
Those who came to Canada since confederation, as well as those who are still coming, will make a point of knowing Canada. Indeed, if the royal commission on biculturalism and
Supply-Privy Council
bilingualism has been instituted, it is because Canada did exist before those people came to live here.

It must be well understood, Mr. Chairman, that the two great races who founded Canada, got along very well in 1867. They contributed to the expansion of the country. But since 1867, another group of people entered the country. Immigration was promoted. The other group settled in Canada and it is always the third party which brings trouble into the family because he does not know really the facts of the matter.

That third group must be educated at all costs-and I am serious when I say that- namely the new Canadians who probably never understood the true meaning of confederation. In fact, I noticed this afternoon that several showed a complete lack of knowledge about confederation because they were not born, in short have not lived, within confederation.
That is why we say today that it is essential to amend confederation, not to destroy it, with regard to that group which came here not to take over confederation but to become part of it.
Immigrants who come to Canada undertake to respect one group or the other, to share its way of living.

And when I hear the New Democratic party members talk about multiculturalism, I say to myself right away that they have never understood the true meaning of confederation, never knew why they were coming to Canada.

I feel that we must look at the inquiry into biculturalism in that light, always to bring up to date, amend and improve confederation, so that every one may use a little of his talent, knowledge and intelligence to understand family life, because I am of the opinion that family life among Canadians is like that of a big city.

A city, where every family has independence and self-determination, when it feels itself in security, because it does not feel its independence threatened by the city council, is a city that will live in peace. Such is the situation of Canada's ten families: if each one is assured of its own security, of its autonomy, of its independence, Canada will live in peace.
I repeat it is in that sense that we must consider the future of confederation, so that neither one of the two groups feels wronged in its rights and feels secure in Canada.

I assure you that if we succeed in convincing everybody of that, by intelligent reasoning instead of by stupid arguments, insults or physical coercion, Canada will be the more powerful and productive.

2272981,ca.proc.d.1964-04-10.27.32,1964-04-10,00163189-b2e2-4300-9100-81f7d68a7930,ca.m.4256,Mr. Horner (Acadia):,,PRIVY COUNCIL,,,I rise to speak on this item with some reservation and some hesitation, due to the very touchy part that biculturalism plays in the economic wellbeing of Canada today.

Certainly, we are all concerned about it. Where is it going? What is Canada going to look like by 1967, 1977, and so on, or by 1987, and one could go on and on. Where is it leading us to? What sound purpose is this inquiry going to bring about? I see here in the estimates that it is already costing something like $300,000. The inquiry we are told is going to continue until 1966, and most likely 1967, when we are going to celebrate our centenary. Is it going to be a happy centenary, or a sad one? Is the inquiry, I wonder, going to promote or bring about a happy centenary? When you see the two chairmen travelling throughout the country listening to interested people presenting their own isolated ideas on biculturalism, I doubt it. In other words, is the inquiry seeking out the thoughts and thinking of the average man on this question, or are they going across the country telling the people their views as to what they think a person should be thinking on this question? We read the opinions of the two chairmen in the various papers, one of them in today's Globe and Mail, where they made a co-operative speech, and they have already summarized their findings, to some extent, in this cooperative speech as far as I can gather. I think the inquiry is costing too much and is doing very little, other than trying to bring a tremendous storm in which Canada can mull about until 1967, and then perhaps thresh out after the whole question dies down and the inquiry has brought down its findings.

It is rather odd that I, the member for Acadia, which has a rather traditional name and is often taken for some part of Canada other than Alberta, should speak on this question. These are my views on this subject and I am certain the vast majority of western Canadians feel as I do. We do not want Canada thrown into a vast turmoil on this touchy subject. We do not want to see Canada split asunder. We firmly believe that our forefathers-and I do not speak entirely of western Canada now-came to this country to establish a new country and start a new culture, not to maintain the two or three cultures which existed in the old country or in the fatherland as the case was. Our forefathers came to this country to escape feudalism as it existed in Ireland, England, France and Europe generally. They

Supply-Privy Council came to this country with the hope of improving their lot and the lot of their families to follow them. They certainly were not interested particularly in the maintenance of any culture they may have left.

I think back to my own constituency. Half of it is called the Palliser triangle. Palliser studied that country to see whether it was fit for civilization-to see whether the land was fit for cultivation. Who settled the country in the ensuing years? Alberta did not become a province until 1905. Who settled that country in the 50 years from the time when Palliser said it was fit for cultivation, or the vast majority of it? Incidentally, he said the part in which I am now living was not fit for cultivation. But in any case it took, not necessarily the two cultures which are today proclaiming that they were the two founding nations to establish Canada; it did not take those two cultures to settle that part of Canada. This part of the country was settled by many different cultures who do not make any boast about trying to maintain their beliefs, their ideals or their language. In many parts of western Canada there are different languages spoken. These people came to Canada to better themselves and to better the following generations. They came to establish a new world and to establish it to the best of their ability, not to quibble about the maintenance of old cultures.

It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that too much of the time of this house is spent in dealing with this touchy subject. We have before us an item of $300,000 which has been spent on this inquiry into biculturalism before the findings of the commission have been made available to us. The cost of this inquiry is likely to run into a million dollars. This commission is not really ascertaining the opinions of Canadians; The members of the commission are giving Canadians their opinion as to what Canada should be like in 1967 and 1968. Certainly we are not going to obtain the co-operation of all the people of Canada by this method.

The hon. member from the eastern part of Canada who preceded me in this debate talked about the inquiry as being nothing less than a gold mine for some people. I do not know who he thought was going to obtain the gold, but it certainly will not be the Canadian people. It may be a political party, it may be the chairmen or it may be somebody else altogether, but it will not be the Canadian people. This commission is doing nothing but harm to the people of Canada. We have heard a lot of talk about the British North America Act of 1867. Certainly this act is a long document containing many words. I have read it all, and I see very little reason to change it in any way. This is
just my opinion, of course. It deals with the subject of biculturalism, it deals with the French language, French laws and the jurisdiction of provinces and the federal government.

I hear too much talk in Canada about biculturalism, too much talk about two states or two nations. I was talking to a constituent of mine not long ago, and he told me about Switzerland. I believe this is an interesting story and has a bearing upon the problem with which we are confronted tonight. He told me that there are three main languages in Switzerland.

2273000,ca.proc.d.1964-04-10.27.51,1964-04-10,20afcc72-88d0-433e-8b61-a7bcd98b2ec9,ca.m.3746,Mr. Mcllrailh:,Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council,PRIVY COUNCIL,,,Mr. Chairman, the reason for this payment to the United States authorities is that at the time the matter was raised it was so late in the season that the assembling and transportation by Canadians of the kind of machinery required to do the job was not possible, if the job was to be done this winter. The United States authorities had the equipment in position, or relatively close to it. That was the underlying reason for it. I made inquiry two days ago to see if I could get a report on the results because I think, as the hon. member well knows, this was an experimental venture to see how feasible it was to keep that road open in the winter, because of many local weather factors with which he is perhaps more familiar than I am but which I have had occasion to study

in other capacities over the last number of years. These are very severe factors. In any event, I was advised that the reports that would give a reasonable indication as to the success or lack of success of the venture were not available. That was earlier this week, in anticipation of this item coming up for discussion.

As to the detailed bills for each month, I do not have them here. The last question the hon. member asked was whether I would give the assurance that we would continue this venture next year. I am quite unable to give that assurance, for the reason that before a decision can be taken to continue the venture next year, we will want to look at the success or failure of the venture this year, analyse how successful it was, what the likely costs will be over the future years in relation to the benefit provided by the road -that is to say, the added facilities that the road has provided-and how many days, notwithstanding the work being done and the machinery available, the road was closed in any event, and what traffic was going through on the road on the days that it was open.

The whole matter will have to be analysed before the government will make a firm commitment for next year. That was another, added reason why I was seeking to find out how much information we had for this year as to the results, because a thorough analysis will have to be made of this project to see whether it is economically wise to spend this amount of money, or whatever amount will be required in future years to do this job.
Therefore as to the last question, I regret that my answer to the hon. member will have to be a categorical no, in the form in which he put his question.

2273002,ca.proc.d.1964-04-10.27.53,1964-04-10,20afcc72-88d0-433e-8b61-a7bcd98b2ec9,ca.m.3746,Mr. Mcllraiih:,Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council,PRIVY COUNCIL,,,Mr. Chairman, as to the inference in the early part of the hon. member's remarks, I can only tell him that I had a great deal to do with this particular matter and am rather familiar with the reasons why the contract was entered into, and all about it. This is the first time I ever heard of any political promise having been made on this subject, or indeed of its having been discussed. I can assure him that if there was any such promise made or anything said on the subject, I certainly did not know about it and it was not known about when this decision was taken; so it has nothing to do with the subject matter.

The question as to whether or not this road should be kept open, is an important one. It is a matter, when we are dealing with these public expenditures, of trying to act responsibly and in a way that will assure that the interests of the taxpayers are protected and their money is used reasonably for the benefit of any section or particular parts of the country. As the hon. member knows, there are very special and difficult problems of transport in the Yukon, and this is a manifestation of one of them.

All I can say to the hon. member is that I assure him this was done to get some experience in this whole field as to whether or not it was feasible to keep this road open in winter. I think it was a very wise and correct decision. It is intended to examine the whole subject before we make a further commitment for another year. All the elements that enter into such considerations will have to be examined before that decision is taken.

2273003,ca.proc.d.1964-04-10.27.54,1964-04-10,8c857bdf-3db5-43c3-8ee0-d33d66a80817,ca.m.3000,Mr. Nielsen:,,PRIVY COUNCIL,,,Mr. Chairman, the minister has, of course, not answered the last question that I put to him, and I will repeat it in just a moment. Perhaps while we are on the relevant item I might mention very briefly a matter which has been brought to the attention of the government by other members of this house, notably the hon. member for Skeena, with respect to the establishment of some sort of arrangement with the United States which would get around the impediment of the Alaskan Panhandle, because as the minister knows by reason of his other experiences apart from his governmental obligations and responsibility, there is a problem in reaching tidewater from the Yukon

Supply-Public Works territory. The only route we have now is by the White Pass and Yukon Railway. Many of us in the Yukon believe that we need a road route through to tidewater. This is the only road route available to us at the moment, and of course its all-weather maintenance is of paramount importance to the economic development of that part of the country. I suggested several years ago that perhaps we might get around it by negotiating with the government of the United States with respect to the establishment of free ports. Perhaps one such location which would be ideal would be Skagway, and another would be Haines Junction. The suggestion has also been made that perhaps we should have corridors not only from the Yukon to tidewater but as well through those portions of the Panhandle which border on the province of British Columbia. I certainly do not wish to create any suggestion whatsoever that I have any objection to the funds being spent. On the contrary, I think they are well spent and in my view the government should continue to maintain the Haines cut-off road on an all-weather basis, even if it means maintaining it by payments to the American government, by wholly American labour at a time of great unemployment in our own country and by the use of American equipment alone.

I think other means could perhaps have been found. We could have employed Canadian workmen on the road. We could have rented Canadian equipment from Canadian contractors in order to maintain the Canadian section of the road for which this money is intended. I know there were particular difficulties that confronted the government at the time and I know that most likely they tried to reconcile matters so they might be able to hire Canadian workmen and equipment for the maintenance of this Canadian road. Nevertheless I am sure that in keeping with the promise they made to the people of the Yukon the government will want to see that the road is maintained next year, and having regard to their desire to reduce unemployment in the country I am equally sure they will want to see it maintained with Canadian workmen next year rather than with American workmen, so that this Canadian money would be going into the economy of that particular part of Canada rather than Canadian funds being paid to a state or federal government of the United States.

The hon. member speaks about this item not being under the defence department estimates. I would remind him that the responsibility for looking after the highway had been in the Department of National Defence because of the construction of the northwest

highway system. This highway was added after the other system was completed, but the military had the kind of establishment there that was capable of doing this kind of work. I think it was the correct decision that they should do so.

2273043,ca.proc.d.1964-04-10.29.4,1964-04-10,8c857bdf-3db5-43c3-8ee0-d33d66a80817,ca.m.3000,Mr. Nielsen:,,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,Yes, the minister informed me that if I did not put the question on the order paper he would have his hon. friend from Vancouver South direct it to him in the house. I have read the answer and I listened to the minister as he gave it, but it still falls far short of satisfying my concern for the safety of general aviation in the vicinity of Calgary airport.

The Department of Transport, through the press and by personal telegrams, has reiterated that these towers would not constitute in any way a danger to aviation using the international airport at Calgary. This is not true. The observations of the department as to the absence of danger apply only to traffic originating under instrument flight rules, traffic which comprises only one quarter of 1 per cent of the traffic using Calgary airport. The submission I make now concerns the attitude of the department in totally ignoring the danger which these towers will present to V.F.R. traffic which comprises 99J per cent of the total traffic going in and out of the airport. It is this traffic to which the towers will constitute a danger.

Any traffic which originates in the Lethbridge or Cowley areas can legally fly toward Calgary with a ceiling of 500 feet and a visibility of one mile. It is patently impossible to see an object such as a radio tower, and take the appropriate action, in the space of one mile if visibility is impaired, say, by showers or falling snow. I do not know whether the minister realizes this or not. He may or may not have flying experience under visual flight rules, but his deputy minister should have this knowledge. The situation becomes all the more dangerous in the Calgary airport where the department's minima for V.F.R. flights are conditions of 500 feet and three miles. The minister should bear in mind that these towers are to be 500 feet above surface level.

One of the procedures used in coming into Calgary, a procedure which most of the pilots flying single V.F.R. flights use, is going to be explained to the minister, now, in the hope that he will make submissions to his officials and, through them, to the C.B.C., that they should cease their determination to go ahead with the construction of these towers. If he is in the northern quadrant, a pilot reports to the Calgary tower at a place near Third Lake and then he comes in on the outer marker, if he is going to use runway 34, and takes a direct course from Third Lake to the outer marker. This course passes within 2,000 feet of the proposed towers and for the Department of Transport to claim that this situation poses no danger at all to V.F.R. aircraft is patently absurd. It is so dangerous for the Department of Transport to hold these views that I think it is almost impossible to arrive intelligently at the conclusion that the towers would create no danger to general aviation in the vicinity.

Calgary international airport has become an attractive airport of entry, if we may call it that, for visual flight rules traffic proceeding northwest to the Yukon, Alaska, and so on. A good deal of that traffic is increasing each year. Adding 500-foot towers on a recognized V.F.R. flyway into Calgary does in no way at all increase the attractiveness of the Calgary international airport for such traffic. It would in fact mean that in marginal weather pilots who were flying on V.F.R. routes would clear Lethbridge or go on to Edmonton, staying well east of Calgary.

We heard the former minister of transport speak about the operations at Penhold and the safety factors there, and we have heard the Minister of National Defence speak on this subject as well. Surely if they claim that general aviation safety is one of their prime concerns, the Minister of Transport should also take these factors into consideration. The minister, while he was holding the portfolio certainly, if not while he was not holding the portfolio, was made aware of a meeting which was held with his officials in Ottawa in November of 1963. This is commonly referred to as the ""Hazards in air space meeting"". Perhaps it was the minister in charge of the privy council, but I cannot recall. At that meeting it was understood and agreed by all groups representing general aviation that the grouping of radio and T.V. towers near any large city into one quadrant or area was a desirable philosophy.

This proposed C.B.C. tower in the vicinity of Calgary international airport violates the principle adopted at that meeting. The contention of the C.B.C. that the Shepard location is the only possible location for their transmission towers is absolute balderdash.

If the state of art of radio wave propagation in Canada is at such a level that the C.B.C. engineers are unable to design a transmitting system in that huge area lying south and west of runway 34 of the Calgary airport, which now contains only five towers, we are indeed suffering a drought of engineering talent, and I do not believe this is actually the case. I think the C.B.C. can find an alternate location which will not present a hazard to general aviation in the vicinity of Calgary international airport, and I think the minister should insist that the C.B.C. engineers look for an alternate location.

It might be argued that V.F.R. pilots will have to change their approaches to Calgary because of these towers. My contention is that this violates the principle that the overall system of controls of airways, regulations and the like, exists for the pilot, not that the pilot exists only for the system. Air line pilots have been reported as saying that these towers will present no hazard to aviation in the area; but I point out to the minister that these air line pilots constitute only a quarter of 1 per cent of the traffic that uses the airport. These V.F.R. pilots put forward a plea, which appears to be falling on deaf ears since not only in this regard is general aviation in the country being neglected but in many other areas as well.

I ask the minister, before this item passes, to give me his assurance that he will accede to the pleas of the several aviation organizations which I know have been in communication with him asking that these towers be relocated in the many, many acres of land available in the vicinity of Calgary international airport. The Alberta aviation council has made representations to the minister, as has the Canadian business aircraft association, the western division of the Canadian owners and pilots association, the international flying farmers, the royal Canadian flying clubs association, and others. Surely these associations that are well versed in aviation matters should be listened to and their recommendations should be considered by the minister in the most favourable light.

Rather than going ahead and insisting on the construction of these towers I think perhaps the minister would be well advised to sit down again with the engineers, or have his officials sit down with the engineers of the C.B.C. to see whether an alternate location cannot be found.
Mr. Chairman, I have just one more point to make to the minister before concluding.

2273051,ca.proc.d.1964-04-10.29.12,1964-04-10,af0c867e-b570-40f2-b26a-5d005e6d5a98,ca.m.3027,Mr. Olson:,,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,Mr. Chairman, this is the first item on this department and I should like to raise a question of great concern to me and to the city of Medicine Hat. I have on occasion during the past few weeks attempted to ask questions on orders of the day about this matter. Perhaps that was not the proper place, but I am happy to see both the present Minister of Transport and his immediate predecessor in the house tonight. The matter I wish to discuss concerns the southern prairie air run.
I have to go into a little history about this air run which is presently completely without

service. As long ago as November 1962 Trans-Canada Air Lines made application to the air transport board to suspend their air service or to be relieved from the obligation to provide a service on the southern prairie air run. The chambers of commerce and city councils of Regina, Swift Current, Medicine Hat and most of the other places concerned raised very serious objections to this at the time. As a result of the air transport board hearings- their findings and recommendations-in February 1963 Trans-Canada Air Lines was granted permission to withdraw from this service because it required the use of two piston engine aircraft, and they claimed they had now converted completely to turbines. Furthermore, TransAir was granted the right to provide this service, particularly from Regina to Swift Current to Medicine Hat to Calgary.

To make a long story short, when TransAir took over this run they were given something like $500,000 worth of equipment by T.C.A. Now, less than a year later, they have suspended the entire service from Regina to Calgary and I understand have reduced the service from Brandon, Dauphin and Yorkton to one flight a week. This is on a Thursday and it used to be a daily run.

Under the agreement between Trans-Canada Air Lines and TransAir there was a transfer of two DC-3 aircraft plus one Viscount aircraft, plus a large amout of other equipment, all for the sum of $1, provided TransAir operated this service for three years. This service has not been provided.

I should like to ask the government what they are doing about getting back this $500,000 worth of equipment, or about demanding payment by TransAir for not fulfilling the terms of the agreement. All of these places I have mentioned are now without air line service of any kind. It happens that in the city of Medicine Hat the federal government is spending $600,000 to renovate one of the runways at the airport, and as I say there is no air line service being operated at the present time. Despite all the representations which have been made to Trans-Canada Air Lines and the air transport board, as well as to the Minister of Transport, no assurance has been given that even after this expenditure has been completed and the renovations concluded air line service will be resumed.

There is something very intriguing about this whole deal, because I know of no indication by Trans-Canada Air Lines that when TransAir applied for the run they would be given any equipment or any subsidy. It is grossly unfair to all of the other air carriers who applied with TransAir for this run in

November 1962. Many of the carriers had laid out some sort of schedule which they were prepared to follow provided the federal government gave them some kind of subsidy. But no subsidy was forthcoming and TransAir offered, according to the decision of the air transport board, the most acceptable kind of service. As I say, when they were granted this franchise, or whatever it should be called, to provide this service T.C.A. transferred to them these three aircraft plus other equipment worth $500,000. If there was some kind of agreement between TransAir and Trans-Canada Air Lines before that date- and I happen to be one who is very suspicious that this was the case-then the submissions made at the air transport board hearings in Regina are shown to be nothing more or less than farcical. Here is $500,000 given to TransAir, and none of the other companies which bid for this run were even aware of it.

Since TransAir has now abandoned this service we have asked Trans-Canada Air Lines if they are prepared to resume it, particularly into the city of Medicine Hat. I have before me a letter addressed to the mayor of the city of Medicine Hat from the president of Trans-Canada Air Lines, and it says this:

Thank you for your letter of February 18 in which you ask that serious consideration be given by T.C.A. to re-establishing its service to Medicine Hat as and when the airport is made suitable for Viscount operations.

To come to what I feel sure is the unwelcome truth at the outset, I can hold out no hope whatever that T.C.A. could resume service to Medicine Hat even if the related airport was made suitable for Viscount operation.
I do not want to read the whole letter, but further on Mr. McGregor says this:

I will not pretend to you that the service represented to T.C.A. anything but a net loss, due to paucity of traffic, but we would have been prepared to continue with cross-subsidization as we do in several other cases, if we had been put in a position where we could use Viscount aircraft.
This is exactly what is taking place in so far as the $600,000 expenditure to extend the runway is concerned. Then, he goes on:

However, now that our ground organization has been disbanded, and in every sense of the word our bridges burned, we could not give serious economic consideration to resuming service to one or more of the original ""prairie run"" stations.

I want to know if there was some kind of deal between Trans-Canada Air Lines and TransAir, some kind of intrigue, before TransAir was given the right to operate this run so that Trans-Canada Air Lines could get out from under it. Clause 13 of the agreement between Trans-Canada Air Lines and TransAir reads as follows:

If TransAir fails to commence the said operations pursuant to clause 12 hereof, TransAir undertakes to pay as liquidated damages to T.C.A. the sum of $500,000 or at the option of TransAir shall return to T.C.A. all the equipment already delivered to TransAir by T.C.A.-

If TransAir commences operation of the aforesaid services pursuant to clause 12 hereof and thereafter discontinues such operation within three years of the said commencement of operations, TransAir undertakes to pay to T.C.A. that proportion of $500,000 which the period from the date of such discontinuance to the date three years after the commencement of operations bears to three years, or at the option of TransAir shall return to T.C.A. such equipment delivered to TransAir by T.C.A. hereunder-
